title: Nimbus Logistics - Service Mesh Egress Proxy & KMS Provenance Review
summary: Deep dive on hybrid private deployment security: proposed pattern is a service-mesh sidecar egress proxy with centralized egress gateway, KMS HSM-backed key provenance for model keys, SOC 2/ISO logging requirements, SSO integration, and data residency controls. Agreed next steps include a network diagram from Redwood, a short benchmark for egress latency, and a security questionnaire with KMS integration notes.

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2028-03-11 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~56m | Attendees: Jordan, Maya (Redwood); Liam, Priya, Eve, Omar (Nimbus)

[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'll hand it over to Maya who will run the technical piece. Quick intro — I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on this account.
[00:18] Maya Singh: Hi all, Maya here, security/infra SE. Today we want to align on a private deployment pattern we recommend for low-latency inference while preserving strong egress controls and key provenance.
[00:30] Liam Chen: Thanks, Maya. High level: Nimbus runs a hybrid fleet — some on GCP us-central, some colocated in EU region. We care about egress controls because of shipper PII and EU residency constraints.
[00:45] Priya Rao: And from security side we need SOC 2 readiness, detailed audit trails for every request to the models, and SSO integration. Also KMS rotation proof, we need chain of custody on keys.
[01:02] Maya Singh: Understood. The pattern we usually propose is a sidecar-based service mesh — envoy sidecars on the model hosts, with a centralized egress gateway per region that performs egress allow-listing, TLS origination with customer-managed certs, and mTLS between mesh components.
[01:25] Omar Haddad: When you say centralized egress gateway, is that a single box or a horizontally scaled cluster? We can't have a single failure point.
[01:35] Maya Singh: Good question. It's a cluster with active-active NAT egress handlers. We use a small egress fleet in the private subnet that does traffic inspection, egress firewall rules, and talks to your CMP for approvals. It's horizontally scaled and can fail over to another region under policy.
[01:52] Priya Rao: Do you support an air-gapped option? Some of our EU workloads must not have ANY outbound to the public internet except through a provable proxy.
[02:04] Jordan Park: Yes — our private deployment supports an airlock pattern. That is, egress must go through your egress proxy which can be an internal proxy we configure; nothing leaves without going through that route. We provide guidance and a sample envoy configuration.
[02:20] Liam Chen: Can you explain how KMS fits in? We need HSM-backed keys with rotation and an audit trail that proves which key signed which model request.
[02:33] Maya Singh: We recommend customer-managed KMS at the control plane boundary. The runtime will hold ephemeral model encryption keys in memory only; wrap keys with your KMS CMKs. For provenance we offer a signing flow: every model binary and artifact is signed by an HSM key and the signatures are stored in the artifact registry plus an append-only audit log.
[02:55] Eve Martinez: Append-only audit log — is that something you host or does it write to our SIEM?
[03:04] Maya Singh: Both options. We can push audit events to your SIEM (syslog/HTTPS) or deliver a signed archive to your S3-compatible store in-region. Events include request metadata, user identity (SSO subject), model version, request id, and KMS key id.
[03:21] Priya Rao: Retention needs: SOC 2 wants 12 months plus exportable CSVs for auditors. ISO might want different granularity. Can we tag events by retention policy?
[03:33] Jordan Park: Yes, we can tag events and apply lifecycle rules. For Private customers we recommend customer-side lifecycle policies but Redwood can also store logs for a paid retention addon.
[03:45] Liam Chen: On RBAC/SSO: we use Okta with SCIM for provisioning. We want role separation so devs can't deploy models to prod. How does Redwood handle RBAC?
[03:58] Maya Singh: We integrate with Okta OIDC for auth + SCIM for provisioning. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (viewer, deployer, admin). For private deployments the control plane can be configured to honor your internal directory via SAML/OIDC and SCIM; tokens are short-lived and audit events include token subject.
[04:20] Omar Haddad: Is there support for step-up auth or MFA for model rollout operations?
[04:27] Maya Singh: We support step-up via SAML assertions; policy engine can require additional approval for rollouts or can be gated behind a separate approval workflow. Those approvals also generate audit events.
[04:40] [00:05:00] Priya Rao: On network segmentation, we want deny-by-default egress. Can you describe the minimal open ports your runtime needs?
[04:54] Maya Singh: Minimal footprint: control plane (inbound from operator) over TLS to our control endpoint on port 443 or a customer-hosted private endpoint; model hosts need to talk to the local egress gateway over mTLS (configurable port), and the egress gateway needs outbound 443 to your approved external endpoints (or none if air-gapped). We'll provide a 1-pager with exact ports.
[05:15] Liam Chen: What about DNS and metadata endpoints? We run IMDS-v2 on our cloud instances and need to ensure sidecars can't hit metadata accidentally.
[05:26] Maya Singh: Sidecars are namespace-isolated and our agent can be configured with egress rules that block instance metadata access; we also support iptables-based policies at host level to block IMDS unless explicitly permitted.
[05:40] [00:10:00] Jordan Park: A quick note about telemetry: we emit per-request metrics but PII is scrubbed by default. Full request payloads never persist in logs unless you opt in. That helps SOC 2 scope.
[05:55] Eve Martinez: We need to know where payloads might persist — does KV cache ever get written to disk?
[06:05] Maya Singh: We keep KV in-memory; persistent cache on disk is only enabled if you opt in for performance and then we recommend disk encryption + KMS-wrapped keys. We'll note defaults in the diagram.
[06:20] [00:15:00] Liam Chen: Let's talk about egress filtering at L7. We want a transparent proxy that does allow-listing by host and path. How would you handle dynamic allow-lists for the models that call out to external tools?
[06:34] Maya Singh: Two-layer approach: mesh sidecar enforces per-service L7 policy; centralized egress gateway enforces global allow-list and performs TLS origination using your certs. For dynamic allow-lists we support a policy API so security team can update rules and they propagate within seconds.
[06:52] Priya Rao: And for outbound file uploads (we have S3 for exports), is the egress flow TLS-terminating at the gateway or using S3 VPC endpoints?
[07:03] Maya Singh: Prefer S3 VPC endpoints where possible. If you require external TLS, the egress gateway can originate TLS to the external service using your certs. We can also do signed uploads using an assumed role pattern so credentials are short lived.
[07:20] [00:20:00] Omar Haddad: Can Redwood's runtime call back to hosted APIs for model telemetry? We prefer all telemetry to stay inside our VPC.
[07:32] Jordan Park: For private deployments telemetry can be pushed to your internal collectors only. Redwood's hosted control plane gets minimal heartbeat info if you choose a hosted control plane; otherwise control plane can be customer-hosted.
[07:46] Priya Rao: For audits, we need an unmodifiable chain — you mentioned append-only; how do you prevent tampering?
[07:55] Maya Singh: We sign audit entries with an HSM-backed key and maintain a Merkle-tree style anchored checkpoint. You can also ship the anchor periodically to your own object store or a notary service. That provides provable immutability.
[08:12] Eve Martinez: That sounds good. Are those signed events human-readable for auditors?
[08:18] Maya Singh: Yes — they include a JSON payload and a signature field. We can provide a verifier tool to reproduce the checkpoint.
[08:28] [00:25:00] Liam Chen: About data residency: if a request originates from EU workload, is there a guarantee model execution and logs stay in-region?
[08:39] Maya Singh: We route by policy: you can pin workloads and models to region, and egress gateways are region-specific. If something has to cross regions, policy-triggered redaction or explicit approval is required.
[08:53] Priya Rao: What about global model cache — sometimes models are cached for performance. How do we keep a EU-only copy?
[09:02] Maya Singh: You can configure cache affinity: cache instances can be region-local only. We have a cache-tagging mechanism so artifacts labeled eu-only won't replicate outside. That will be in the network and artifact diagram.
[09:18] [00:30:00] Omar Haddad: Let's discuss failover. If an egress gateway goes down, what's the behavior for in-flight requests?
[09:29] Maya Singh: The mesh sidecar will failover to the next healthy gateway according to policy. For in-flight requests the behavior depends on timeouts — we recommend short retry policies to avoid duplicate side effects, and for idempotent ops we use idempotency keys.
[09:45] Jordan Park: Also note: Canary rollouts can be pinned to a control-plane that is separate for staging vs prod. That reduces blast radius.
[09:56] Priya Rao: Compliance question: can audit logs include SSO subject and Okta group membership at time of request?
[10:05] Maya Singh: Yes, we capture Okta subject and group claims via OIDC at token issuance time. Group membership snapshot is included in the audit event.
[10:18] [00:35:00] Liam Chen: How do you handle KMS key rotation events? Auditors want proof that key rotation occurred and old signatures remain verifiable.
[10:30] Maya Singh: We keep a key version history and the audit includes KMS key id and key version used to wrap/unwrapped. Signatures are verifiable because they're accompanied by the signing key id and we preserve the public key for historical verification. If you use an HSM with attestation, we can include attestation statements.
[10:46] Eve Martinez: Attestation — do you integrate with common HSM vendors?
[10:51] Maya Singh: We integrate with common cloud KMS vendors like Google Cloud KMS, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and on-prem HSMs via PKCS#11. Attestation with TPM or Cloud HSM is supported where vendor provides it.
[11:05] [00:40:00] Jordan Park: A quick note on data-in-transit: all control plane traffic is mTLS; runtime traffic between sidecars and the egress gateway is mTLS; and egress gateways can be configured to use customer-managed certs or certs from your PKI.
[11:21] Priya Rao: For firewalling, we also need L4 restrictions — can we enforce both policy layers?
[11:28] Maya Singh: Absolutely. The host-level firewall can enforce L4 deny-by-default and the mesh enforces L7. We recommend defense-in-depth: iptables or cloud security groups plus sidecar policies.
[11:40] Liam Chen: One last technical: do you run any privileged sidecar containers or do they run unprivileged?
[11:47] Maya Singh: Sidecars run unprivileged by default. Any operations that need elevated privileges are brokered through a limited privileged operator with strict RBAC and audit trails.
[11:58] [00:50:00] Omar Haddad: Ok — this was great. Quick recap of outstanding concerns: 1) ensure EU-only cache and logs, 2) HSM attestation and provenance for model signing, 3) deny-by-default egress with per-region gateways, 4) SCIM/Okta mapping details.
[12:16] Jordan Park: Exactly. We'll send the diagram and the KMS/HSM note. Maya will follow up with a deeper network playbook and we'll schedule the infra-only deep dive for the week of the 21st.
[12:30] Priya Rao: I also want a quick checklist for auditors — SOC 2 items mapped to Redwood controls.
[12:37] Jordan Park: We'll produce a SOC 2 control mapping doc and attach sample audit events.
[12:45] Eve Martinez: Thanks everyone.
[12:49] Liam Chen: Thanks.
[12:52] Jordan Park: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email with the artifacts. End of call.

Optional attachments mentioned in call: network-diagram-draft (to be sent), kms-provenance-one-pager (to be sent), soc2-control-mapping (to be sent)
